---
title: "Python → MapLibre Bridge"
subtitle: "Bringing data from a Python cell to a reactive map"
---

## What this bridge is

Python **has no idea MapLibre exists**. A Python cell returns plain
GeoJSON — a `dict`, or the equivalent of a GeoDataFrame — as its last
expression; an `{ojs}` cell reads that value and draws it on the map.
No package to install, no "map" object to build on the Python side.

The practical advantage is the same as before: you can add a layer or
update data **without reloading the whole map** — every cell you run
only updates the source it writes to, and the map already visible
below stays right where it is.

## The map on this page

It's created only once, when the page opens. The Python cells further
down update it incrementally — they don't recreate it.

<div id="bridge-map" style="height: 400px; width: 100%; border: 1px solid #5a4f3e;"></div>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bridgeMap = {
  const m = new WebGeoDS.Map("bridge-map", {
    center: [12.4964, 41.9028], // Rome
    zoom: 5,
    style: "https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/positron"
  });
  await m.ready();
  return m;
}
```

## The two parts of the bridge

### 1. The Python cell — return GeoJSON, not a map object

```python
{"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [
    {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"name": "Rome"}, "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [12.4964, 41.9028]}}
]}
```

No special `import`, no package to install: it's a plain Python
`dict`, the cell's last expression. With a `GeoDataFrame` (geopandas)
it's just as direct — `gdf.__geo_interface__` produces the same
structure, properties included (verified: unlike
`gdf.geometry.__geo_interface__`, which returns empty `properties:
{}`, you need to use the whole GeoDataFrame, not just its geometry
column). If the CRS isn't already WGS84, it needs to be reprojected
first — `__geo_interface__` doesn't do that on its own:

```python
gdf.to_crs(epsg=4326).__geo_interface__
```

### 2. `getCellValue` + `setGeoJSON` — read and draw

```js
value = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("my-cell-id", Generators)
{
  if (value) await myMap.setGeoJSON("my-source", value);
}
```

`WebGeoDS.getCellValue(cellId, Generators)` (defined in
`shared/code-cell.js`) reactively observes the current value of a
Python/R cell identified by its id; `sharedMap.setGeoJSON(sourceId,
data, options)` (`shared/map.js`) draws it — creates the source/layer
if they don't exist yet, otherwise just updates the data. No queue of
calls to replay, no delta tracking: it's just "read the current
value, show it".

::: {.callout-note}
**Watch out for state**: it isn't the Python cell that "remembers"
what's on the map, it's the **source** — it stays exactly as it is
until you update it (another `setGeoJSON()` on the same id) or clear
it (`setGeoJSON(id, {type: "FeatureCollection", features: []})`).
Re-running the same Python cell with the same result does nothing
new; running it with a different result updates the source, without
ever recreating the map.
:::

## Example 1 — a source with one point

```{.webgeods-python #bridge-cell-1}
{"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [
    {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"name": "Rome"}, "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [12.4964, 41.9028]}}
]}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bridgeCell1 = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("bridge-cell-1", Generators)
{
  if (bridgeCell1) await bridgeMap.setGeoJSON("bridge-points", bridgeCell1);
}
```

## Example 2 — updating the same source with more points

Same `"bridge-points"` source as Example 1: it doesn't recreate it,
it updates it — `setGeoJSON()` calls `source.setData()` when the
source already exists.

```{.webgeods-python #bridge-cell-2}
{"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [
    {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"name": "Rome"}, "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [12.4964, 41.9028]}},
    {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"name": "Milan"}, "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [9.19, 45.4642]}}
]}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bridgeCell2 = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("bridge-cell-2", Generators)
{
  if (bridgeCell2) await bridgeMap.setGeoJSON("bridge-points", bridgeCell2);
}
```

## Example 3 — restyling: a JS job, not a Python one

Changing the color or radius of the points isn't a question about
the data — Python has nothing to say here. The `{ojs}` cell decides
it directly, calling the native MapLibre instance exposed by
`sharedMap.map` (no dedicated method needed for a case this
straightforward):

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
restyleBridgePoints = {
  const button = document.createElement("button");
  button.textContent = "Color the points terracotta";
  button.onclick = () => {
    bridgeMap.map.setPaintProperty("bridge-points", "circle-color", "#b0522c");
    bridgeMap.map.setPaintProperty("bridge-points", "circle-radius", 10);
  };
  return button;
}
```

${restyleBridgePoints}

This is the central point of the model: **Python answers "what is
this data", JS decides "what should the user see of it"**. Neither
language needs to know about the other beyond this boundary.

## Reference — the part of `map.js` relevant here

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| `setGeoJSON(sourceId, data, options)` | Creates the source/layer if it doesn't exist, otherwise just updates the data. `options.paint` sets the style ONLY at creation time. |
| `getGeoJSON(sourceId)` | Reads back the GeoJSON currently on the source. |
| `addMarkers(sourceId, options)` / `clearMarkers(sourceId)` | Markers on a subset of features (`options.filter`/`options.property`). |
| `highlight(sourceId, featureIds)` / `clearHighlights(sourceId)` | Highlights specific features on a dedicated layer, without touching the base style. |

For anything more specific than these, `sharedMap.map` is the native
MapLibre GL JS instance — no wrapper to work around.
